newsitem.title: MEXICO: FORECAST-Volumes key in Maseca, Gruma 1996 results.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Volumes key in Maseca, Gruma 1996 results.

text.p: Food analysts said they will pay close attention to the production volume of Mexican tortilla and corn flour maker Maseca when fourth-quarter results come out some time in mid-February.

As for Gruma, Maseca's less actively traded holding company, the fourth-quarter results are expected to be the first that fully show the benefits of the joint ventures with the Archer Daniels Midland Co in August 1996.

Three analysts consulted by Reuters said one of their chief concerns was how much Maseca, the world's largest producer of corn flour and tortillas, can improve on its 1995 fourth quarter production of 443,000 tonnes of corn flour.
An average of the three analysts' earning per share estimates is 0.70 pesos for Maseca and 3.67 pesos for Gruma. In 1995, Maseca posted an EPS of 0.48 pesos and Gruma 4.28 pesos.

"It's a volume story right now. I'm looking for 20 percent volume growth," said Kevin Kirkeby, a food analyst with Robert Fleming in New York. "That's generally what they've been averaging the past few quarters."

"I'd like to see some good volume growth," added Will Landers, a food and beverage analyst with Lehman Brothers in New York. "Although looking forward to 1997, I think it's going to slow down compared to 1996."
Sales volumes, however, are not seen growing in kind with production volumes because of lower corn prices resulting from the easing of drought conditions in the United States and Mexico.

Los Angeles-based analyst Greg Rianhard of D.A. Campbell said Maseca's sales volume growth rates are likely to be tempered by the slowing shift from the traditional method of tortilla production to the corn-flour method.

Maseca benefitted from the trend in 1996 of abandoning the traditional method of boiling and milling to make tortillas. Instead, with corn flour, Mexicans just add water. Analysts see the trend continuing but on a slower pace when there are better harvests.

"Their sales revenue will look smaller compared to the third quarter," said Robert Fleming's Kirkeby. "But that's not something to be concerned about because their gross profit per tonne will be the same."
When it comes to Gruma, analysts said they will focus on its U.S. operations to see how Gruma fared in the still-growing tortilla market.

"The margin expansion for their U.S. operations is going to be the issue," Landers said. "There have been a number of complaints in the U.S. Their margins have tended to lag a little bit around 5 to 6 percent when people are looking for 6 or 7. I don't think it will be that high but something around 5.5 to 6 percent."

In a conference call following release of 1995 results, Gruma's chief financial officer, Javeir Velez, said Gruma was expecting seven percent growth in the "established" tortilla markets like California, with growth in the "underdeveloped" tortilla markets of the Northeast to be "much higher."
"I would say that in dollar terms, that's a pretty fair number (seven percent)," Kirkeby said. "The tortilla market is still showing very strong growth as is corn flour."

In August, Gruma and ADM said they agreed to form joint ventures in the U.S. corn flour and Mexican wheat flour markets. Under the deal, Gruma received $258 million, which is used to retire short-term debts. That is expected to drastically reduce Gruma's interest payments in the fourth quarter.
ADM got 74.7 million new Gruma shares, representing a 22 percent stake in Gruma.
Gruma also issued 20 million new shares in the fourth quarter, so its earnings per share are likely to fall, analysts said.
D.A. Campbell's Rianhard, however, said any dilution resulting from the new shares issued will be largely offset by the reduced interest payments.
